title.rhyme: Chapter 1: In Peach Garden, three brothers' oath is sworn; 'Gainst Yellow Turbans, merit first is borne.
title.prose: Chapter 1: At the Peach Garden Banquet, three heroes swear brotherhood; slaying the Yellow Turbans, heroes earn their first merit.
title.original: 第一回：宴桃園豪傑三結義，斬黃巾英雄首立功

paragraphs.original: 詞曰：滾滾長江東逝水，浪花淘盡英雄。是非成敗轉頭空：青山依舊在，幾度夕陽紅。白髮漁樵江渚上，慣看秋月春風。一壺濁酒喜相逢：古今多少事，都付笑談中。
paragraphs.prose: The lyric says: The rolling waters of the Yangtze flow eastward, their waves washing away all heroes. Right and wrong, success and failure—turn the head, and all is empty: the green mountains still remain as before; how many times has the setting sun glowed red? White-haired fishermen and woodcutters upon the river's isles have grown accustomed to watching the autumn moon and the spring breeze. A jug of unstrained wine, the joy of meeting once more: of the many affairs of ages past and present, all are consigned to laughter and idle talk.
paragraphs.rhyme:
Thus sings the lyric of the Yangtze's flow,
Whose waves have washed the heroes long ago.
Both right and wrong, success and loss are vain;
A turn of head, and naught shall here remain.
Yet ageless still the verdant mountains stand,
How oft the sunset's blaze has stained the land!
The hoary fishers, woodmen on the shore,
Watch springtime breezes, autumn moons pass o'er.
With cloudy wine, glad friends together meet;
All deeds of ages melt in laughter sweet.

paragraphs.original: 話說天下大勢，分久必合，合久必分：周末七國分爭，并入於秦。及秦滅之後，楚、漢分爭，又并入於漢。漢朝自高祖斬白蛇而起義，一統天下。後來光武中興，傳至獻帝，遂分為三國。推其致亂之由，殆始於桓、靈二帝。桓帝禁錮善類，崇信宦官。及桓帝崩，靈帝即位，大將軍竇武、太傅陳蕃，共相輔佐。時有宦官曹節等弄權，竇武、陳蕃謀誅之，作事不密，反為所害。中涓自此愈橫。
paragraphs.prose: It is said: the great trend of the empire — long divided, it must unite; long united, it must divide. At the end of the Zhou dynasty, the Seven States contended, and were absorbed into Qin. After Qin was destroyed, Chu and Han contended, and were in turn absorbed into Han. The Han dynasty, from when Gaozu raised an uprising by killing the white serpent, unified the realm. Later came the Guangwu Restoration, and the line passed down to Emperor Xian, whereupon it was divided into the Three Kingdoms. Tracing the cause of this disorder, it likely began with the two emperors Huan and Ling. Emperor Huan imprisoned virtuous men and trusted eunuchs. When Emperor Huan died and Emperor Ling ascended the throne, the Grand General Dou Wu and the Grand Tutor Chen Fan together served as his regents. At that time the eunuch Cao Jie and his fellows abused their power; Dou Wu and Chen Fan plotted to put them to death, but their plans were not kept secret, and they were themselves struck down. From this time onward, the palace attendants grew ever more domineering.
paragraphs.rhyme:
Such is the tide of empires, since of old:
Long-split, they merge; long-merged, they break and fold.
At Zhou's last age, the Seven States made war,
Till victor Qin engulfed them, near and far.
When Qin had fall'n, came Chu and Han to fray,
Till Han alone bore off the laurel'd day.
For Han's great [Founder](char-emperor-gaozu) slew the serpent white,
And raised the loyal arms in righteous fight.
Then [Guangwu](char-emperor-guangwu)'s arm restored the falling crown,
And bore it long, through ages of renown.
Till, passed to wretched Xian, the realm did break,
And split in three — three kingdoms in its wake.
Whence rose this woe? Behold its source malign —
'Twas Huan and [Ling](char-emperor-ling), the start of Han's decline.
For Huan the worthy bound in fetters fast,
And to the eunuch crew his trust he cast.
When Huan was dead, young [Ling](char-emperor-ling) assumed the throne;
Dou Wu and Chen Fan made his cause their own.
But [Cao Jie](char-cao-jie), eunuch, ruled with cunning hand;
Dou Wu and Chen Fan plotted to withstand —
Yet, in their plotting, careless of disguise,
Themselves they fell, beneath the eunuch's eyes.
From this dread hour the palace eunuchs grew,
And o'er the throne their fatal shadow threw.

paragraphs.original: 建寧二年四月望日，帝御溫德殿。方陞座，殿角狂風驟起，只見一條大青蛇，從梁上飛將下來，蟠於椅上。帝驚倒，左右急救入宮，百官俱奔避。須臾，蛇不見了。忽然大雷大雨，加以冰雹，落到半夜方止，壞卻房屋無數。建寧四年二月，洛陽地震；又海水泛溢，沿海居民，盡被大浪捲入海中。光和元年，雌雞化雄。六月朔，黑氣十餘丈，飛入溫德殿中。秋七月，有虹見於玉堂；五原山岸，盡皆崩裂。種種不祥，非止一端。
paragraphs.prose: On the full-moon day of the fourth month of the second year of Jianning, the Emperor held court in the Wende Hall. Just as he ascended his throne, a violent gale arose from the corner of the hall; a great green serpent was seen flying down from the beams above, and coiled itself upon his chair. The Emperor fell back in fright; his attendants rushed him into the inner palace, while all the hundred officials fled in panic. In a moment, the serpent vanished. Suddenly there came a great thunderstorm, accompanied by hail, which did not cease until midnight, destroying countless dwellings. In the second month of the fourth year of Jianning, Luoyang was struck by an earthquake; the sea overflowed, and the inhabitants of the coast were all swept into the ocean by the great waves. In the first year of Guanghe, a hen changed into a cock. On the first day of the sixth month, a black vapor more than ten zhang in length flew into the Wende Hall. In the seventh month of autumn, a rainbow appeared in the Jade Hall; and the cliffs of the Wuyuan Mountains all collapsed and split asunder. Such ill omens came in many kinds, not in one alone.
paragraphs.rhyme:
In [Jianning](misc-jianning)'s second year, fourth moon's full light,
Young [Ling](char-emperor-ling) ascended Wende's hall of might.
Just as he sat, a sudden tempest blew,
And from the beams a great green serpent flew,
And coiled itself upon the royal seat;
The startled king fell back, in pale retreat.
His servants bore him quickly to his rest;
The hundred lords fled all, in dread distressed.
The serpent vanished, gone as if a dream;
Then thunder rolled, and rain fell down in streams.
With hail till midnight's hour, the tempest played,
And countless dwellings in the dust were laid.
Two years from then, in [Jianning](misc-jianning)'s fourth, the ground
At [Luoyang](loc-luoyang) quaked with hollow rumbling sound.
The seas o'erflowed; the dwellers by the strand
Were swept by waves, far from the living land.
In [Guanghe](misc-guanghe)'s first, the omens grew more strange:
A hen took on the cock — yin-yang's exchange.
In sixth moon's first, a vapor black and tall
Flew straight to Wende, and the royal hall.
In autumn's seventh moon, a rainbow shone
Within the Jade Hall, where its arch was thrown.
And on the cliffs of Wuyuan, lofty, grand,
The slopes were rent, and broke on every hand.
Such omens, ill, of every varied kind,
Were not in one, but many, intertwined.

paragraphs.original: 帝下詔問群臣以災異之由，議郎蔡邕上疏，以為蜺墮雞化，乃婦寺干政之所致，言頗切直。帝覽奏歎息，因起更衣。曹節在後竊視，悉宣告左右。遂以他事陷邕於罪，放歸田里。後張讓，趙忠，封諝，段珪，曹節，候覽，蹇碩，程曠，夏惲，郭勝十人朋比為奸，號為「十常侍」。帝尊信張讓，呼為「阿父」，朝政日非，以致天下人心思亂，盜賊蜂起。
paragraphs.prose: The Emperor issued an edict, asking the assembled ministers the cause of these calamities. The Court Counselor Cai Yong submitted a memorial, in which he held that the falling rainbow and the hen-turned-cock were the consequences of palace women and eunuchs meddling in affairs of state; his words were exceedingly forthright. The Emperor read the memorial and sighed, and then rose to change his garments. Cao Jie, watching from behind, observed all and reported it to his fellows. They thereupon implicated Cai Yong in other charges and banished him back to his country home. Later, ten men—Zhang Rang, Zhao Zhong, Feng Xu, Duan Gui, Cao Jie, Hou Lan, Jian Shuo, Cheng Kuang, Xia Yun, and Guo Sheng—joined together in conspiracy, taking the name of "the Ten Attendants." The Emperor placed his trust above all in Zhang Rang, addressing him as "Father"; the affairs of state grew daily worse, until the hearts of the realm yearned for rebellion, and bandits swarmed like bees.
paragraphs.rhyme:
The king, alarmed, an edict sent to court,
To ask his lords whence rose each strange report.
Cai Yong, the counselor, sent up a scroll
And named the cause, forthright in word and soul:
"'Tis women's hand and eunuchs' baleful sway
That call these dread portents in dark array."
The king perused the scroll, then gave a sigh;
Rose up, his robe to change, and pass'd thereby.
[Cao Jie](char-cao-jie), who lurked behind, had marked it all,
And told his fellows in the eunuch hall.
On other charge they laid him in disgrace,
And drove him home, to country's barren place.
Anon ten eunuchs joined in vile design,
[Zhang Rang](char-zhang-rang), [Zhao Zhong](char-zhao-zhong), [Feng Xu](char-feng-xu), of foul line;
[Duan Gui](char-duan-gui), [Cao Jie](char-cao-jie), [Hou Lan](char-hou-lan), and [Jian Shuo](char-jian-shuo) too,
[Cheng Kuang](char-cheng-kuang), [Xia Yun](char-xia-yun), [Guo Sheng](char-guo-sheng) — a baleful crew.
"The Ten Attendants" — so the band was styled,
A wicked clique, who policies defiled.
The king, deluded, gave [Zhang Rang](char-zhang-rang) his trust,
And called him "Father", sunk in folly's dust.
The court grew daily worse, in foul decay;
The realm entire long'd for rebellion's way.
And bandits bee-like rose, on every hand,
Till peace had vanished from the troubled land.

paragraphs.original: 時鉅鹿郡有兄弟三人：一名張角，一名張寶，一名張梁。那張角本是個不第秀才。因入山採藥，遇一老人，碧眼童顏，手執藜杖，喚角至一洞中，以天書三卷授之，曰：「此名太平要術。汝得之，當代天宣化，普救世人；若萌異心，必獲惡報。」角拜問姓名。老人曰：「吾乃南華老仙也。」言訖，化陣清風而去。
paragraphs.prose: At that time, in the commandery of Julu there lived three brothers: one named Zhang Jiao, one Zhang Bao, and one Zhang Liang. This Zhang Jiao was originally a scholar who had failed the imperial examinations. Once, having entered the mountains to gather medicinal herbs, he met an old man with green eyes and a youthful face, holding a goosefoot staff in his hand, who called Jiao into a cave and there bestowed upon him three scrolls of a Heavenly Book, saying: "This is called the Essential Arts of Great Peace. Now that you have obtained it, you must on heaven's behalf spread its teachings and bring deliverance to all the people of the world; should you harbor any wayward intent, you shall surely receive evil retribution." Jiao bowed and asked his name. The old man said: "I am the Old Immortal of Nanhua." Having spoken, he transformed into a gust of pure wind and was gone.
paragraphs.rhyme:
In Julu's bounds there dwelt the brothers three:
[Zhang Jiao](char-zhang-jiao), [Zhang Bao](char-zhang-bao), [Zhang Liang](char-zhang-liang), one family.
This [Jiao](char-zhang-jiao), a scholar who had failed his test,
Roamed up the hills, where mountain herbs grow best.
There met he, in a glade by leafy way,
A sage with eyes of green and face of May.
He held a staff of goosefoot in his hand,
And led the youth into a cavern grand,
Where three rare scrolls of Heaven's lore he gave,
And spoke these words, his counsel deep and grave:
"Behold these Taiping Arts of lore divine,
That charge thee with the work of Heaven's design.
'Tis thine to spread their light, the world to win;
But should ill aim arise, dread doom begin."
[Jiao](char-zhang-jiao) bowed, and asked his name. The sage replied:
"Old Immortal of Nanhua — none beside."
He spake; and chang'd to wind, away was flown;
The cave was empty — [Jiao](char-zhang-jiao) stood there alone.

paragraphs.original: 角得此書，曉夜攻習，能呼風喚雨，號為太平道人。中平元年正月內，疫氣流行，張角散施符水，為人治病，自稱大賢良師。角有徒弟五百餘人，雲游四方，皆能書符念咒。次後徒眾日多，角乃立三十六方，─大方萬餘人，小方六七千─，各立渠帥，稱為將軍。訛言「蒼天已死，黃天當立。」又云「歲在甲子，天下大吉。」令人各以白土，書「甲子」二字於家中大門上。青、幽、徐、冀、荊、揚、兗、豫八州之人，家家侍奉大賢良師張角名字。角遣其黨馬元義，暗齎金帛，結交中涓封諝，以為內應。角與二弟商議曰：「至難得者，民心也。今民心已順，若不乘勢取天下，誠為可惜。」遂一面私造黃旗，約期舉事；一面使弟子唐州，馳書報封諝。唐州乃逕赴省中告變。帝召大將軍何進調兵擒馬元義，斬之；次收封諝等一干人下獄。
paragraphs.prose: Jiao obtained this book and studied it day and night, until he could summon wind and call rain, and styled himself the Daoist of Great Peace. In the first month of the first year of Zhongping, pestilence ran abroad in the land. Zhang Jiao went about distributing talismanic water and healing the sick, calling himself the Great Worthy Teacher. Jiao had more than five hundred disciples, who wandered the four quarters like roaming clouds, all able to inscribe talismans and chant incantations. Their numbers grew daily, until Jiao organized them into thirty-six divisions—the large divisions counting more than ten thousand men, the small six or seven thousand—each under its own chief, whom they styled General. They falsely proclaimed: "The Azure Heaven is dead; the Yellow Heaven shall arise." They also said: "When the year is jiazi, all under heaven shall be greatly blessed." Jiao ordered every man to write the two characters 'jiazi' in white clay upon the gate of his home. Throughout the eight provinces of Qing, You, Xu, Ji, Jing, Yang, Yan, and Yu, household by household, the people gave worship to the name of the Great Worthy Teacher Zhang Jiao. Jiao sent his accomplice Ma Yuanyi, secretly bearing gold and silks, to win over the eunuch Feng Xu, who was to act as their agent within the palace. Jiao took counsel with his two brothers, saying: "What is hardest to win is the hearts of the people. Now that the hearts of the people are with us, if we do not ride this tide to seize all under heaven, it would truly be a thing to regret." He therefore on one hand privately made yellow banners and set a date for the rising; on the other, he dispatched his disciple Tang Zhou with a letter to inform Feng Xu. But Tang Zhou went straight to the imperial chancery and revealed the plot. The Emperor summoned the Grand General He Jin to muster troops, who seized Ma Yuanyi and beheaded him; next they took Feng Xu and the rest of his fellows and cast them into prison.
paragraphs.rhyme:
[Jiao](char-zhang-jiao) took the book; both day and night he scann'd,
And could the wind and rain at will command.
'The Taiping Daoist' was the name he bore;
In [Zhongping](misc-zhongping)'s first, the pestilence swept o'er,
He gave the sick his charm-blest waters free,
'Wise and Worthy Master' he claim'd to be.
Five hundred pupils thronged at his command,
And roamed the four wide quarters of the land.
All skilled in talisman and chanted spell,
They spread his name in every road and dell.
He formed thirty-six bands; each captain wore
The name of 'General' — chief in rebel war.
They cried, in falsehood: 'Lo! The Azure dies!
The Yellow Heaven shall in glory rise!'
'When [jiazi](misc-jiazi) comes, all bliss the world shall know!'
They bade each door '[jiazi](misc-jiazi)' in white clay show.
In eight wide provinces — [Qing](loc-qing-province), [You](loc-you-province), [Xu](loc-xu-province), [Ji](loc-ji-province),
[Jing](loc-jing-province), [Yang](loc-yang-province), [Yan](loc-yan-province), [Yu](loc-yu-province) — to him each house bent knee.
Now [Jiao](char-zhang-jiao) sent Ma Yuanyi with sacks of gold,
To bribe [Feng Xu](char-feng-xu), the eunuch base and bold.
[Jiao](char-zhang-jiao) spake: 'No prize so hard to gain as hearts;
'Twere shame to spurn this tide, ere chance departs.'
He bade the yellow flags arise on high,
And sent Tang Zhou with writ to [Feng Xu](char-feng-xu) hie.
But Tang Zhou false the secret straight betrayed,
And to the court the rebel plot displayed.
The king sent [He Jin](char-he-jin)'s troops with martial might;
Yuanyi was caught, beheaded in their sight.
[Feng Xu](char-feng-xu) and all his fellows captive made,
And to the dungeon-cells in chains were laid.

paragraphs.original: 張角聞知事露，星夜舉兵，自稱天公將軍，─張寶稱地公將軍，張梁稱人公將軍─。申言於眾曰：「今漢運將終，大聖人出﹔汝等皆宜順從天意，以槳太平。」四方百姓，裹黃巾從張角反者，四五十萬。賊勢浩大，官軍望風而靡。何進奏帝火速降詔，令各處備禦，討賊立功；一面遣中郎將盧植，皇甫嵩，朱雋，各引精兵，分三路討之。
paragraphs.prose: Zhang Jiao, learning that his plot had been exposed, raised his army in the dead of night, styling himself the General of the Lord of Heaven; Zhang Bao styled himself the General of the Lord of Earth, and Zhang Liang the General of the Lord of Men. He proclaimed to the multitude: "Now the fortunes of Han are nearing their end; a great sage has come forth. You should all obey the will of heaven, that we may usher in the age of great peace." From every quarter the common people, wrapping yellow turbans about their heads, joined Zhang Jiao in revolt, to the number of four or five hundred thousand. So vast was the rebels' force that the imperial armies fell back at the very sight of them. He Jin memorialized the Emperor to issue an edict with all speed, commanding every region to prepare its defenses and to win merit by quelling the rebels; at the same time, the Generals of the Household Lu Zhi, Huangfu Song, and Zhu Jun were dispatched, each leading picked troops, to march in three columns against the foe.
paragraphs.rhyme:
[Jiao](char-zhang-jiao), hearing all his secret plot was bared,
By starlight took up arms, for war prepared.
As 'General of Heaven' [Jiao](char-zhang-jiao) took rise;
[Bao](char-zhang-bao) 'of the Earth', [Liang](char-zhang-liang) 'of Mankind' likewise.
He cried: 'The Han now fails; a sage is here!
Obey ye Heaven's will; Taiping draws near.'
From every land, in turbans yellow dressed,
Some half a million answered his behest.
So vast the rebel host, the king's troops broke,
And scattered, fearing every rebel stroke.
[He Jin](char-he-jin) informed the king of urgent need,
Who quickly issued forth a royal deed,
He bade each region brace its walls and gate,
And win renown by quelling rebel state.
Three captains marched: [Lu Zhi](char-lu-zhi) the bold and just,
[Huangfu Song](char-huangfu-song), and [Zhu Jun](char-zhu-jun), in royal trust.
Each led picked troops, in three divided ways,
To smite the foe and earn the empire's praise.

paragraphs.original: 且說張角一軍，前犯幽州界分。幽州太守劉焉，乃江夏竟陵人氏，漢魯恭王之後也；當時聞得賊兵將至，召校尉鄒靖計議。靖曰：「賊兵眾，我兵寡，明公宜作速招軍應敵。」劉焉然其說，隨即出榜招募義兵。榜文行到涿縣，乃引出涿縣中一個英雄。
paragraphs.prose: Now Zhang Jiao's army first invaded the borders of Youzhou. The Grand Administrator of Youzhou, Liu Yan, was a native of Jingling in Jiangxia, and a descendant of Prince Gong of Lu of the Han. Hearing that the rebel forces were drawing near, he summoned the Colonel Zou Jing for counsel. Said Jing: "Their numbers are great, our forces few; Your Excellency should at once raise volunteers to meet them." Liu Yan agreed, and issued forthwith a proclamation to enroll righteous troops. The proclamation reached Zhuo county, and there it called forth a hero of that place.
paragraphs.rhyme:
[Zhang Jiao](char-zhang-jiao)'s first host on [You](loc-you-province)'s far border lay,
Where [Liu Yan](char-liu-yan) ruled, his arm's far-reaching sway.
Of Jiangxia's Jingling sprang this lordly man,
A scion of the Lu King's princely clan.
He, hearing tidings that the foes drew near,
Called [Zou Jing](char-zou-jing), captain — his advice to hear,
Said [Jing](char-zou-jing): "Their host is great, our forces few;
Your Lord should haste to muster levies new."
The lord agreed; abroad his notice spread,
To call brave volunteers, by valor led,
The writ to [Zhuo](loc-zhuo) town came, and forth it brought
A hero of that town, in honor wrought.

paragraphs.original: 那人不甚好讀書；性寬和，寡言語，喜怒不形於色；素有大志，專好結交天下豪傑；生得身長七尺五寸，兩耳垂肩，雙手過膝，目能自顧其耳，面如冠玉，脣若塗脂；中山靖王劉勝之後，漢景帝閣下玄孫﹔姓劉，名備，字玄德。昔劉勝之子劉貞，漢武時封涿鹿亭侯，後坐酬金失侯，因此遺這一枝在涿縣。玄德祖劉雄，父劉弘。弘曾舉孝廉，亦嘗作吏，早喪。玄德幼孤，事母至孝；家貧，販屨織蓆為業。家住本縣樓桑村。其家之東南，有一大桑樹，高五丈餘，遙望之，童童如車蓋。相者云：「此家必出貴人。」
paragraphs.prose: This man was not greatly fond of books; his nature was generous and mild; he was sparing of speech, and showed neither joy nor anger upon his face; he had always cherished great ambitions, and was particularly devoted to making friends with the bold spirits of the realm. He stood seven chi and five cun tall, his ears hanging down to his shoulders and his hands reaching below his knees; his eyes could behold his own ears; his face was as a jade beneath a coronet, and his lips as though daubed with vermilion. He was a descendant of Liu Sheng, Prince Jing of Zhongshan, and the great-great-grandson of the Emperor Jing of Han; his surname was Liu, his given name Bei, and his courtesy name Xuande. Long ago, Liu Sheng's son Liu Zhen had in the time of the Emperor Wu been enfeoffed as Lord of Zhuolu Pavilion, but afterwards, falling under the laws concerning the gold-tribute, he lost his lordship; and thus this branch of the family had been left behind in Zhuo county. Xuande's grandfather was Liu Xiong, his father Liu Hong. Liu Hong had been put forward as 'Filial and Incorrupt', and had served as a minor official, but died young. Xuande was orphaned in his childhood and served his mother with the utmost filial piety. His family was poor, and they made their living by selling straw sandals and weaving mats. He lived in the village of Lousang in his county. To the south-east of his house there stood a great mulberry tree, more than five zhang in height; from afar it stretched lush and round, like the canopy of a chariot. A fortune-teller had said: "From this family must surely come forth a man of noble rank."
paragraphs.rhyme:
This man set little prize on books and lore;
He spake but few, and showed no smile or sore.
His nature mild and gen'rous, broad and kind,
An even temper, a forbearing mind.
Yet vast ambition warmed his quiet breast;
He sought all heroes, kindred to the best.
Seven chi five he stood, of figure tall;
Two ears like pendants to the shoulders fall.
The hands beyond the knees in length descend;
The eyes themselves can to his own ears bend.
A face like jade beneath the crown's bright shine,
The lips like roses, dipped in crimson wine.
Of Liu Sheng's stock, the Prince of Zhongshan's race;
The fourth descent from Jing of Han his place.
Liu was his surname, [Bei](char-liu-bei) the given name.
Liu Sheng his son, Liu Zhen, in Wu's high reign,
Was crowned Pavilion-Lord of Zhuolu plain,
But fell by gold-tribute from lord's estate;
And thus in [Zhuo](loc-zhuo) this branch was left to fate.
His grandsire Xiong, his father Hong, were known;
For Hong, by filial fame, to rank had grown,
To office held, but soon to death was led;
Young [Bei](char-liu-bei), an orphan, his good mother fed,
With utmost filial care, in tender heed,
He serv'd his mother well, in word and deed.
In life of poverty he plied his trade:
Sold straw sandals and mats his hands had made.
In Lousang lived he, in his county's bound:
South-east a great mulberry was renown'd,
Five zhang in height, its crown like cart spread wide,
A leafy canopy on every side.
A seer beheld and said: "This house shall raise
A man of noble rank, in coming days."

paragraphs.original: 玄德幼時，與鄉中小兒戲於樹下，曰：「我為天子，當乘此車蓋。」叔父劉元起奇其言，曰：「此兒非常人也！」因見玄德家貧，常資給之。年十五歲，母使游學，嘗師事鄭玄、盧植；與公孫瓚等為友。及劉焉發榜招軍時，玄德年己二十八歲矣。當日見了榜文，慨然長歎。隨後一人厲聲言曰：「大丈夫不與國家出力，何故長歎？」
paragraphs.prose: In his youth, Xuande would play with the village children beneath this tree, saying: "When I am Son of Heaven, I shall ride a chariot with such a canopy." His uncle, Liu Yuanqi, marveling at his words, declared: "This boy is no common child!" And seeing Xuande's family in poverty, he often gave them aid. At fifteen, his mother sent him forth to study, and he studied for a time under the teachers Zheng Xuan and Lu Zhi, and was friends with Gongsun Zan and others. By the time Liu Yan issued the proclamation calling up troops, Xuande was already eight-and-twenty. That day, having seen the writ, he gave forth a long, heavy sigh. Whereupon a man behind him said in a stern voice: "When a true man does not exert himself for his country, wherefore should he sigh so long?"
paragraphs.rhyme:
In boyhood, sporting with his village host,
Beneath this mulberry, he made this boast:
'When I am king,' he said, 'I'll ride one day,
With canopy like this in proud array.'
His uncle Yuanqi marvelled, much impressed,
And cried: 'This child shall rise above the rest.'
And, seeing [Bei](char-liu-bei) in poverty's deep need,
Sustained the youth with kind, paternal heed.
At fifteen years, his mother bade him roam,
To study with the sages, far from home.
He learned from Zheng Xuan, and [Lu Zhi](char-lu-zhi) the wise;
With [Gongsun Zan](char-gongsun-zan) grew friends, with kindred ties.
When [Liu Yan](char-liu-yan)'s writ went forth to call up men,
Was [Bei](char-liu-bei) full eight-and-twenty years by then.
That day he saw the writ, and sighed full long,
With heart that ached, no aid to lend the throng.
A voice behind cried out, in stern reply:
"A man, slow to serve — why heave this long sigh?"

paragraphs.original: 玄德回視其人：身長八尺，豹頭環眼，燕頷虎鬚，聲若巨雷，勢如奔馬。玄德見他形貌異常，問其姓名。其人曰：「某姓張，名飛，字翼德。世居涿郡，頗有莊田，賣酒屠豬，專好結交天下豪傑。適纔見公看榜而歎，故此相問。」玄德曰：「我本漢室宗親，姓劉，名備。今聞黃巾倡亂，有志欲破賊安民；恨力不能，故長歎耳。」飛曰：「吾頗有資財，當招募鄉勇，與公同舉大事，如何？」玄德甚喜，遂與同入村店中飲酒。
paragraphs.prose: Xuande turned to look at the man: he stood eight chi tall, with a leopard's head and round eyes, the jaw of a swallow and whiskers of a tiger; his voice like a great clap of thunder, his bearing like a galloping horse. Seeing that the man's form was extraordinary, Xuande asked his name. He answered: "My surname is Zhang, my given name Fei, my courtesy name Yide. For generations my family has dwelt in Zhuo commandery, where I have a fair holding of land; I sell wine and butcher pigs, and especially love to make friends with the bold spirits of the realm. Just now, seeing you sigh at the proclamation, I asked the cause." Xuande replied: "I am of the imperial clan of Han, surnamed Liu, named Bei. Hearing now that the Yellow Turbans have risen in rebellion, I have set my heart on crushing them and bringing peace to the people; but I lament that my strength does not suffice—and so I sighed." Said Fei: "I have some means at hand, and might call up the village braves; if you and I joined in this great enterprise, how say you?" Xuande was greatly pleased, and the two went together to a village inn to drink.
paragraphs.rhyme:
[Liu Bei](char-liu-bei) then turned, beheld a stranger high,
Eight chi he stood, with martial gleam of eye.
A leopard's head, and round his eyeballs rolled,
With swallow-jaw and tiger-whiskers bold.
His voice broke forth as thunder's awful roar;
Like steed at gallop, fierce his stance he bore.
[Liu Bei](char-liu-bei), in wonder at this form so strange,
Asked of his name. The man made full exchange:
"My surname Zhang, my given name is Fei,
Yide my style. In [Zhuo](loc-zhuo) my fathers stay.
Some farm I hold; I sell wine, butcher swine,
And love to seek out heroes, friends of mine.
Just now I marked you sighing at the call:
Wherefore your heart so deeply held in thrall?"
[Liu Bei](char-liu-bei) replied: "I am of Han's high race;
Liu Bei my name, sprang of imperial place.
Now hearing how the Yellow Turbans rise,
I burn to crush the rebels and chastise —
But ah! My strength suffices not the foe;
Therefore I sighed, with sorrow long and slow."
Said [Fei](char-zhang-fei): "I have some means — a goodly store;
We'll raise the village braves and march to war."
[Liu Bei](char-liu-bei) was glad; the two, with one accord,
Sought out a village inn, where wine they poured.

paragraphs.original: 正飲間，見一大漢，推著一輛車子，到店門首歇了；入店坐下，便喚酒保：「快斟酒來吃，我待趕入城去投軍。」玄德看其人：身長九尺，髯長二尺：面如重棗，脣若塗脂；丹鳳眼，臥蠶眉：相貌堂堂，威風凜凜。玄德就邀他同坐，叩其姓名。其人曰：「吾姓關，名羽，字壽長，後改雲長，河東解良人也。因本處勢豪，倚勢凌人，被吾殺了；逃難江湖，五六年矣。今聞此處招軍破賊，特來應募。」玄德遂以己志告之。雲長大喜。同到張飛莊上，共議大事。
paragraphs.prose: As they were drinking, they saw a great fellow pushing a cart, who halted at the door of the inn and came in to sit. He called to the server: "Pour me some wine, and quickly—I am hastening into the city to enlist in the army." Xuande looked at him: he stood nine chi tall, with a beard two chi long; his face was like dark jujube, his lips as though daubed with rouge; he had eyes like a vermilion phoenix and brows like silkworms at rest; his appearance was stately, his bearing awe-inspiring. Xuande invited him to sit with them and asked his name. The man said: "My surname is Guan, my given name Yu, my courtesy name Shouchang—afterwards changed to Yunchang. I am a man of Jieliang in Hedong. There was a powerful man of that place who relied on his might to oppress others, and I slew him; I have been wandering the rivers and lakes some five or six years. Now, hearing that troops were being raised here to crush the rebels, I have come to enlist." Xuande told him his own purpose, and Yunchang was overjoyed. Together they went to Zhang Fei's farmstead to take counsel of the great affair.
paragraphs.rhyme:
While yet they drank, a mighty fellow came,
With cart in hand, and stopped before the same.
He sat, and to the wine-boy loud he cried:
"Quick, pour me wine — to city I must ride!"
Nine chi he stood, with beard two chi in length,
A face like dark ripe jujube, full of strength.
Lips touched in rouge, with eyes of phoenix' fire,
With silkworm brows, a bearing stern of ire.
[Liu Bei](char-liu-bei) invites him: "Pray, with us partake.
What is thy name?" The man did answer make:
"Guan is my surname, Yu my given name;
First Shouchang my style, then Yunchang became.
In far Hedong, in Jieliang, I was born;
A man oppressed his neighbors with his scorn,
This wretch I slew; and ever since my flight,
Five years and more I've wandered, day and night.
And hearing here brave men were call'd to fight,
I came on purpose, to enlist outright."
[Liu Bei](char-liu-bei) then told his purpose; glad was he;
To [Fei](char-zhang-fei)'s own farmstead went the comrades three.

paragraphs.original: 飛曰：「吾莊後有一桃園，花開正盛；明日當於園中祭告天地，我三人結為兄弟，協力同心，然後可圖大事。」玄德、雲長、齊聲應曰：「如此甚好。」次日，於桃園中，備下烏牛白馬祭禮等項，三人焚香，再拜而說誓曰：「念劉備、關羽、張飛，雖然異姓，既結為兄弟，則同心協力，救困扶危；上報國家，下安黎庶；不求同年同月同日生，但願同年同月同日死。皇天后土，實鑒此心。背義忘恩，天人共戮。」誓畢，拜玄德為兄，關羽次之，張飛為弟。祭罷天地，復宰牛設酒，聚鄉中勇士，得三百餘人，就桃園中痛飲一醉。來日收拾軍器，但恨無馬匹可乘。
paragraphs.prose: Fei said: "Behind my farmstead lies a peach garden, where the blossoms are now in full flower. Tomorrow, let us go thither and offer sacrifice to Heaven and Earth, that we three may swear ourselves brothers, and join our hearts and our strength as one; thereafter we may plan the great enterprise." Xuande and Yunchang answered with one voice: "Excellent indeed." On the morrow, in the peach garden, they made ready the rites with a black bull, a white horse, and the other offerings; the three burned incense, bowed twice, and spoke their oath: "We, Liu Bei, Guan Yu, and Zhang Fei, though of different surnames, having now sworn ourselves brothers, will unite our minds and strength to relieve the troubled and succour the endangered; above, to repay the nation; below, to bring peace to the common folk. We do not ask to be born in the same year, the same month, the same day; but we pray to die in the same year, the same month, the same day. Imperial Heaven and Sovereign Earth, bear witness to this our heart; should any of us forsake duty or forget kindness, may Heaven and men together strike him down." The oath ended, they bowed: Xuande as elder brother, Guan Yu next, and Zhang Fei the youngest. The sacrifice to Heaven and Earth being done, they slaughtered cattle, set out wine, and gathered the village braves, gaining more than three hundred men; in the peach garden they all drank deeply, to drunkenness. The next day they set in order their weapons of war—but they grieved that they had no horses to ride.
paragraphs.rhyme:
Said [Fei](char-zhang-fei): "Behind my farm a peach grove fair
With blossoms full; to-morrow we'll repair,
And there, before the gods, sworn brothers stand,
To join in heart and arm, in soul and hand."
With one accord, the two assented straight:
"It is well said — appoint the morrow's date."
Next day, in peach-bloom shade, with black bull whole,
White horse, and rites prepared, they bowed in soul,
And spake their oath: "We three of diff'rent name,
[Liu Bei](char-liu-bei), [Guan Yu](char-guan-yu), [Zhang Fei](char-zhang-fei) — now share one frame.
United, hearts and arms shall succour bear:
To save the troubled, lift the people's care.
Above, our country's grace we will repay;
Below, the common folk's distress allay.
We seek no birth on one same year and tide,
But pray to die together, side by side.
But if one prove him false to vow and kin,
May Heav'n and men together end his sin."
The oath thus done, they bowed: [Liu Bei](char-liu-bei) the chief,
[Yu](char-guan-yu) second, [Fei](char-zhang-fei) the third, in age most brief.
They slew the kine, set wine, and gathered round
Three hundred village braves — at one accord bound.
They drank to drunkenness, the day prolonged;
Prepared their arms — but yet for steeds they longed.

paragraphs.original: 正思慮間，人報「有兩個客人，引一夥伴儅，趕一群馬，投莊上來。」玄德曰：「此天佑我也！」三人出莊迎接。原來二客乃中山大商：一名張世平，一名蘇雙，每年往北販馬，近因寇發而回。玄德請二人到莊，置酒管待，訴說欲討賊安民之意。二客大喜，願將良馬五十匹相送；又贈金銀五百兩，鑌鐵一千斤，以資器用。玄德謝別二客，便命良匠打造雙股劍。雲長造青龍偃月刀，又名冷豔鋸，重八十二斤。張飛造丈八點鋼矛。各置全身鎧甲。共聚鄉勇五百餘人，來見鄒靖。鄒靖引見太守劉焉。三人參見畢，各通姓名。玄德說起宗派，劉焉大喜，遂認玄德為姪。
paragraphs.prose: As they were thus pondering, a man came to report: "Two strangers, with a band of comrades, are driving a herd of horses toward the farmstead." Said Xuande: "This is Heaven aiding me!" The three went out to greet them. The two visitors were great merchants of Zhongshan: one called Zhang Shiping, the other Su Shuang. Each year they went north to trade in horses, but had lately turned homeward because of the rebel uprising. Xuande led them to the farmstead, set out wine to entertain them, and told them of his desire to put down the rebels and bring peace to the people. The two visitors were greatly pleased, and offered fifty fine horses; they also gave five hundred liang of gold and silver, and a thousand jin of fine steel, for the making of weapons. Xuande thanked the visitors and parted from them, then ordered skilled smiths to forge a pair of twin swords. Yunchang had made for himself the Green Dragon Crescent Blade—also called the Cold-Splendour Saw—weighing eighty-two jin. Zhang Fei had wrought a Snake-Pointed Steel Spear of one zhang and eight chi. Each of them was furnished with full armor. Together, they gathered more than five hundred village braves, and came to wait upon Zou Jing, who in turn brought them before the Grand Administrator Liu Yan. When the three had paid their respects and exchanged names, Xuande told of his lineage, and Liu Yan was greatly pleased, and recognized him as his nephew.
paragraphs.rhyme:
Whilst yet they pondered, news to hand was brought:
"Two strangers driving steeds the farmstead sought."
"This is Heaven's gift!" [Liu Bei](char-liu-bei) cried with cheer;
The brothers three went out their guests to hear.
Two merchants of Zhongshan came in their train:
Zhang Shiping and Su Shuang, of merchant strain.
Each year they took their horses north to trade;
But rebels rose, and southward flight they made.
[Liu Bei](char-liu-bei) received them, wine and feast was spread,
And told his goal — to crush the rebel's head.
The merchants, joyed at heart, bestowed in praise
Some fifty horses, fit for warlike days.
Five hundred liang of gold and silver fine,
A thousand jin of steel, for arms divine.
[Liu Bei](char-liu-bei), with thanks, dismissed each merchant guest,
A twin-blade pair he bade his smiths invest.
[Guan Yu](char-guan-yu)'s Green Dragon Crescent Blade was made,
"Cold-Splendour Saw" — at eighty-two jin laid.
[Fei](char-zhang-fei) forged a spear of pointed steel, well-honed;
One zhang and eight chi long — in hand enthroned.
All three with full-suit armor stood prepared;
Five hundred braves to [Zou Jing](char-zou-jing)'s camp they fared.
[Zou Jing](char-zou-jing) then led them forth to [Liu Yan](char-liu-yan)'s hand;
They bowed, and named themselves before his stand,
[Liu Bei](char-liu-bei) declared his line; [Liu Yan](char-liu-yan) was warmed,
And owned him nephew, kindred ties confirmed.

paragraphs.original: 不數日，人報黃巾賊將程遠志統兵五萬來犯涿郡。劉焉令鄒靖引玄德等三人，統兵五百，前去破敵。玄德等欣然領軍前進，直至大興山下，與賊相見。賊眾皆披髮，以黃巾抹額。當下兩軍相對，玄德出馬，─左有雲長，右有翼德─，揚鞭大罵：「反國逆賊，何不早降！」
paragraphs.prose: Within a few days, a man came to report that the Yellow Turban general Cheng Yuanzhi was leading fifty thousand troops to invade Zhuo. Liu Yan commanded Zou Jing to take Xuande and his two brothers, with five hundred troops, and go forth to break the foe. Xuande and his companions gladly led their men out, and came to the foot of Mount Daxing, where they faced the rebels. The rebels wore their hair loose and bound their foreheads with yellow scarves. As the two armies stood drawn up against each other, Xuande rode forth—Yunchang at his left and Yide at his right—and lifting his whip he cried in a great voice: "Traitors to the realm—why do you not surrender now?"
paragraphs.rhyme:
In few days came report: the foe drew near,
[Cheng Yuanzhi](char-cheng-yuanzhi)'s hordes — five myriads of fear.
[Liu Yan](char-liu-yan) bade [Zou Jing](char-zou-jing) march, with troops to dare,
[Liu Bei](char-liu-bei) and brothers led five hundred there.
Glad were they all to march with brave intent;
To Daxing's foot their warlike steps they bent.
There stood the foe — loose-haired, with turbans tied
Of yellow band, in countless ranks supplied.
The two great armies faced; [Liu Bei](char-liu-bei) rode out,
With [Guan Yu](char-guan-yu) left, with [Zhang Fei](char-zhang-fei) right about,
He raised his whip, and shouted to the foe:
"Vile traitors — why not yield and bow ye low?"

paragraphs.original: 程遠志大怒，遣副將鄧茂出戰。張飛挺丈八蛇矛直出，手起處，刺中鄧茂心窩，翻身落馬。程遠志見折了鄧茂，拍馬舞刀，直取張飛。雲長舞動大刀，縱馬飛迎。程遠志見了，早吃一驚；措手不及，被雲長刀起處，揮為兩段。後人有詩讚二人曰：英雄發穎在今朝，一試矛兮一試刀。初出便將威力展，三分好把姓名標。
paragraphs.prose: Cheng Yuanzhi, in great wrath, sent his deputy Deng Mao out to battle. Zhang Fei thrust forth his eighteen-chi serpent-spear and rushed straight out; at the lift of his hand, he pierced Deng Mao through the heart, and the man tumbled rolling from his saddle. Cheng Yuanzhi, seeing Deng Mao struck down, lashed his horse and brandished his sabre, and rode straight at Zhang Fei. But Yunchang, swinging his great blade, galloped forth to meet him. Cheng Yuanzhi, at the sight, was already taken aback; before he could lift his hand to strike, Yunchang's blade swept down and clove him in two. Later men composed a poem in praise of the two: "The heroes display their mettle this very morn; one tries the spear, the other tries the blade. At their first sally they unfold their might; in the threefold realm shall their names be well set down."
paragraphs.rhyme:
[Cheng Yuanzhi](char-cheng-yuanzhi), sore enraged, sent forth his man:
Deng Mao, his deputy, the field he ran.
[Zhang Fei](char-zhang-fei) rushed forth with snake-spear, swift and dread,
Pierced Deng Mao through the heart — he fell, struck dead.
The rebel chief, when Deng Mao fallen lay,
Spurred horse and saber, sought [Zhang Fei](char-zhang-fei) to slay.
But [Guan Yu](char-guan-yu), swinging his great blade, drew near;
And [Cheng](char-cheng-yuanzhi), beholding, started back in fear,
Too late to raise his arm — [Yu](char-guan-yu)'s blade arose,
And cleft him sheer in two, with mighty blows.
A later bard, in honor of the twain,
Composed this song, their glory to maintain:
"Two heroes show their mettle on this morn,
One tries the spear, the other blade well-borne.
At their first stride, dread power they unfold;
In three-fold realms, their names shall be enrolled."

paragraphs.original: 眾賊見程遠志被斬，皆倒戈而走。玄德揮軍追趕，投降者不計其數，大勝而回。劉焉親自迎接，賞勞軍士。次日，接得青州太守龔景牒文，言黃巾賊圍城將陷，乞賜救援。劉焉與玄德商議。玄德曰：「備願往救之。」劉焉令鄒靖將兵五千，同玄德，關，張，投青州來。賊眾見救軍至，分兵混戰。玄德兵寡不勝，退三十里下寨。玄德謂關、張曰、「賊眾我寡，必出奇兵，方可取勝。」乃分關公引一千軍伏山左，張飛引一千軍伏山右，鳴金為號，齊出接應。
paragraphs.prose: The rebels, seeing Cheng Yuanzhi beheaded, all turned their weapons and fled. Xuande led his troops in pursuit; those who surrendered were beyond reckoning, and they returned in great triumph. Liu Yan came in person to receive them, and rewarded the soldiers. The next day, a dispatch came from Gong Jing, Grand Administrator of Qingzhou, saying that the Yellow Turbans had surrounded his city, which was on the verge of falling, and begging for relief. Liu Yan took counsel with Xuande. Xuande said: "I, Bei, am willing to go to their rescue." Liu Yan ordered Zou Jing to take five thousand troops, with Xuande, Guan, and Zhang, and march to Qingzhou. When the rebels saw the relief army approach, they split their forces and fought in disorder. Xuande's troops were too few to prevail, and he withdrew thirty li to encamp. Xuande said to Guan and Zhang: "The rebels are many and we are few; we must use stratagem if we are to gain the victory." He thereupon divided the force: Lord Guan was to lead a thousand men in ambush on the left of the hill, Zhang Fei a thousand on the right; when the gong sounded as signal, they would sally forth together to give support.
paragraphs.rhyme:
The rebels, when their captain fell, gave way,
Reversed their arms, and fled the fatal day.
[Liu Bei](char-liu-bei) pursued; the foes in numbers yield;
A glorious triumph filled the bloody field.
[Liu Yan](char-liu-yan) in person came their host to greet,
And to the soldiers gave reward complete.
Next day a dispatch came from [Qingzhou](loc-qing-province)'s lord:
[Gong Jing](char-gong-jing), beset by rebels, aid implored.
[Liu Yan](char-liu-yan) with [Liu Bei](char-liu-bei) talked the matter o'er;
Said [Liu Bei](char-liu-bei): "Let me go to wage this war."
[Liu Yan](char-liu-yan) to [Zou Jing](char-zou-jing) gave five thousand strong,
With [Bei](char-liu-bei) and brothers in the warlike throng.
To [Qingzhou](loc-qing-province) marched they; soon the foe drew nigh,
Who, splitting forces, fell on them with cries.
Outmatched, [Liu Bei](char-liu-bei) gave back, the field unwon;
Thirty li back retired, his camp begun.
[Liu Bei](char-liu-bei) to [Yu](char-guan-yu) and [Fei](char-zhang-fei): "The foes are vast,
Our numbers small; on craft our hopes are cast."
He ordered [Yu](char-guan-yu), with thousand men, to lie
On hill's left side; [Fei](char-zhang-fei) right, with watchful eye:
At gong-clash give the signal; from each side
Together rush, and stem the rebel tide.

paragraphs.original: 次日，玄德與鄒靖，引軍鼓譟而進。賊眾迎戰，玄德引軍便退。賊眾乘勢追趕，方過山嶺，玄德軍中一齊鳴金，左右兩軍齊出，玄德麾軍回身復殺。三路夾攻，賊眾大潰。直趕至青州城下，太守龔景亦率民兵出城助戰。賊勢大敗，剿戮極多，遂解青州之圍。後人有詩讚玄德曰：運籌決算有神功，二虎還須遜一龍。初出便能垂偉績，自應分鼎在孤窮。
paragraphs.prose: On the next day, Xuande and Zou Jing led the troops forward with drums and shouts. The rebels came out to meet them in battle, and Xuande's army then turned and fell back. The rebels, seizing the chance, pressed in pursuit; and just as they crossed the ridge, the gong sounded throughout Xuande's army, and the left and right divisions sortied together, while Xuande wheeled his troops about and slew anew. Caught between three columns, the rebel host was utterly broken. They drove the foe straight up to the walls of Qingzhou, where Grand Administrator Gong Jing himself led the city's militia out to join the fight. The rebel force was crushed outright, and great was the slaughter; and so the siege of Qingzhou was lifted. Later men composed a poem in praise of Xuande: "In planning and decision he wrought as one divine; / two tigers still must yield to a single dragon. / At his first sortie he could already leave a mighty deed; / fitting it is that he should share the tripod, though in solitary poverty."
paragraphs.rhyme:
Next day [Liu Bei](char-liu-bei) and [Zou Jing](char-zou-jing) led the way,
With drum and clamor onward to the fray.
The rebels charged; [Liu Bei](char-liu-bei) drew back his force,
And lured the foe along the chosen course.
The rebels chased; they passed the ridge in zeal,
When sudden gongs sent forth a clarion peal.
From left and right the ambush forces broke,
While [Liu Bei](char-liu-bei) wheeled, and answered stroke for stroke.
Caught in three columns, rebel ranks were crushed,
And, breaking, headlong from the field they rushed.
They drove the wreck to [Qingzhou](loc-qing-province)'s outer wall;
[Gong Jing](char-gong-jing) led forth his levies to the brawl.
The rebel host was broken, hewn and slain,
And [Qingzhou](loc-qing-province) freed; the city breathed again.
A later poet sang [Liu Bei](char-liu-bei) in lays,
Whose echo through the ages keeps his praise:
"He planned and reckoned with a power divine;
Where dragons fly, two tigers must resign.
His maiden field a mighty triumph showed;
Though poor, he'd share the realm by fate bestowed."

paragraphs.original: 龔景犒軍畢，鄒靖欲回。玄德曰：「近聞中郎將盧植與賊首張角戰於廣宗，備昔曾師事盧植，欲往助之。」於是鄒靖引軍自回，玄德與關、張引本部五百人投廣宗來。至盧植軍中，入帳施禮，具道來意。盧植大喜，留在帳前聽調。
paragraphs.prose: When Gong Jing had finished feasting the troops, Zou Jing wished to return. Xuande said: "I have lately heard that the General of the Household Lu Zhi is engaged with the rebel chief Zhang Jiao at Guangzong; I formerly studied under Lu Zhi, and would go to his aid." Zou Jing thereupon led his army back, while Xuande, with Guan and Zhang, took his original five hundred men and marched to Guangzong. Coming to Lu Zhi's camp, he entered the tent, paid his respects, and set forth his purpose in full. Lu Zhi was greatly pleased, and kept him at the headquarters tent to await orders.
paragraphs.rhyme:
When [Gong Jing](char-gong-jing)'s feast had cheered the host content,
[Zou Jing](char-zou-jing) his thoughts to homeward course had bent.
But [Liu Bei](char-liu-bei) said: "[Lu Zhi](char-lu-zhi) at Guangzong's plain
Engages [Zhang Jiao](char-zhang-jiao) with both might and main.
He was my teacher in my early years;
I'd march, and aid him 'gainst those rebel spears."
[Zou Jing](char-zou-jing) turned back, and led his troops away;
[Liu Bei](char-liu-bei) to Guangzong led his small array.
To [Lu Zhi](char-lu-zhi)'s camp he came, and bowed his head;
His purpose to the chief he plainly said.
[Lu Zhi](char-lu-zhi) rejoiced, and kept him close at hand,
Awaiting orders at the chief's command.

paragraphs.original: 時張角賊眾十五萬，植兵五萬，相拒於廣宗，未見勝負。植謂玄德曰：「我今圍賊在此，賊弟張梁，張寶在潁川，與皇甫嵩、朱雋對壘。汝可引本部人馬，我更助汝一千官軍，前去潁川打探消息，約期剿捕。」玄德領命，引軍星夜投潁川來。時皇甫嵩、朱雋領軍拒賊，賊戰不利，退入長社，依草結營。嵩與雋計曰：「賊依草結營，當用火攻之。」遂令軍士，每人束草一把，暗地埋伏。其夜大風忽起。二更以後，一齊縱火，嵩與雋各引兵攻擊賊寨，火燄張天，賊眾驚慌，馬不及鞍，人不及甲，四散奔走。殺到天明，張梁、張寶引敗殘軍士，奪路而走。
paragraphs.prose: At that time Zhang Jiao's host of one hundred and fifty thousand and Lu Zhi's troops of fifty thousand stood opposed at Guangzong, and the issue had not yet been decided. Lu Zhi said to Xuande: "I am here besieging the rebels. The rebel chief's younger brothers, Zhang Liang and Zhang Bao, are at Yingchuan, where they stand opposed to Huangfu Song and Zhu Jun. You may take your own troops—I shall furnish you besides with a thousand of the imperial soldiers—and go on to Yingchuan to gather word, that we may fix a date for the rebels' suppression." Xuande received the order, and led his army by night to Yingchuan. At that time Huangfu Song and Zhu Jun were leading their troops against the rebels; the rebels, faring ill in the fight, withdrew into Changshe and made their camp upon a thicket of grass. Song and Jun took counsel: "The rebels have made their camp upon grass; we must attack them with fire." They thereupon ordered every soldier to bind a torch of straw, and to lie in secret ambush. That night a great wind suddenly arose. After the second watch they together set the blaze, and Song and Jun each led their troops to assault the rebel camp. The flames stretched to the very heavens; the rebels were thrown into panic, and—their horses unsaddled, their men without armor—scattered to all four sides and fled. The slaughter went on till dawn, when Zhang Liang and Zhang Bao, gathering the broken remnants of their men, forced a road and made their escape.
paragraphs.rhyme:
[Zhang Jiao](char-zhang-jiao) led fifteen myriads to the war;
[Lu Zhi](char-lu-zhi) five myriads stood at Guangzong's door.
The two great armies locked in fierce array,
And neither yet could win the doubtful day.
[Lu Zhi](char-lu-zhi) to [Liu Bei](char-liu-bei) spoke: "I hold the foe
Hard pressed at Guangzong; thou shalt straightway go
To Yingchuan, where [Liang](char-zhang-liang) and [Bao](char-zhang-bao) now contend
'Gainst [Song](char-huangfu-song) and [Jun](char-zhu-jun): a thousand troops I'll lend,
That thou mayst learn the rebels' present plight,
And fix a day to overthrow their might."
[Liu Bei](char-liu-bei) obeyed, and led his troops away;
By night they marched to Yingchuan, no delay.
There [Song](char-huangfu-song) and [Jun](char-zhu-jun) the rebel host had spurned;
The foe, repulsed, to Changshe's quarter turned.
And there they pitched their camp where grass grew tall,
And reedy thickets fenced them like a wall.
Said [Song](char-huangfu-song) and [Jun](char-zhu-jun): "On grass their camp is bound;
With fire we'll burn the rebels to the ground."
Each man a torch of straw bound fast and tight,
And, hid in ambush, waited for the night.
That night a sudden wind arose and grew;
Past second watch, in concert, fires they threw.
[Song](char-huangfu-song) marched, and [Jun](char-zhu-jun), against the rebel lair;
The flames climbed up, and reached the heavens' stair.
The rebels, stricken, broke in wild dismay:
Bare horse, bare man, they scattered all away.
The slaughter raged till dawn at last appeared;
[Liang](char-zhang-liang), [Bao](char-zhang-bao), with broken bands, a passage cleared.

paragraphs.original: 忽見一彪軍馬，盡打紅旗，當頭來到，截往去路。為首閃出一將，身長七尺，細眼長髯；官拜騎都尉；沛國譙郡人也：姓曹，名操，字孟德。操父曹嵩，本姓夏侯氏；因為中常侍曹騰之養子，故冒姓曹。曹嵩生操，小字阿瞞，一名吉利。操幼時，好游獵，喜歌舞；有權謀，多機變。操有叔父，見操游蕩無度，嘗怒之，言於曹嵩。嵩責操。操忽心生一計：見叔父來，詐倒於地，作中風之狀。叔父驚告嵩，嵩急視之，操故無恙。嵩曰：「叔言汝中風，今己愈乎？」操曰：「兒自來無此病；因失愛於叔父，故見罔耳。」嵩信其言。後叔父但言操過，嵩並不聽。因此，操得恣意放蕩。
paragraphs.prose: All at once there appeared a column of cavalry, every banner red, that came up at the head and cut across their line of march. From the van there sprang forth a general seven chi in stature, with narrow eyes and a long beard; in office he held the rank of Cavalry Commandant; he was a man of Qiao Commandery in the Principality of Pei: surnamed Cao, named Cao, style Mengde. Cao's father, Cao Song, was originally of the Xiahou clan, but, having been adopted by the Permanent Attendant Cao Teng, he took the surname Cao. Cao Song begat Cao, whose childhood name was Aman, and who was also called Jili. In his youth Cao loved the hunt and delighted in song and dance; he was full of stratagems and quick of cunning shifts. He had an uncle who, seeing his nephew's unbridled wantonness, would often grow angry and lay the matter before Cao Song; and Cao Song would reprimand Cao. One day Cao struck upon a scheme: seeing his uncle approach, he feigned to fall to the ground in the seizure of a stroke. The uncle, alarmed, hurried to tell Cao Song, and Cao Song came in haste—but Cao was as well as ever. Cao Song said: "Your uncle says you had a stroke; are you now recovered?" Cao said: "I have never been so afflicted; my uncle has lost his affection for me, and so misrepresents me thus." Cao Song believed him. Thereafter, whenever the uncle reported any fault of Cao's, Cao Song would no longer give ear; and so Cao was free to indulge himself at will.

paragraphs.original: 時人有橋玄者，謂操曰：「天下將亂，非命世之才，不能濟。能安之者，其在君乎？」南陽何顒見操，言：「漢室將亡，安天下者，必此人也。」汝南許劭，有知人之名。操往見之，問曰：「我何如人？」劭不答。又問，劭曰：「子治世之能臣，亂世之奸雄也。」操聞言大喜。年二十，舉孝廉，為郎，除洛陽北都尉。初到任，即設五色棒十餘條於縣之四門。有犯禁者，不避豪貴，皆責之。中常侍蹇碩之叔，提刀夜行，操巡夜拏住，就棒責之。由是，內外莫敢犯者，威名頗震。後為頓丘令。因黃巾起，拜為騎都尉，引馬步軍五千，前來潁川助戰。正值張梁、張寶敗走，曹操攔住，大殺一陣，斬首萬餘級，奪得旗旛、金鼓馬匹極多。張梁、張寶死戰得脫。操見過皇甫嵩，朱雋，隨即引兵追襲張梁、張寶去了。
paragraphs.prose: There was a man of his time named Qiao Xuan, who said to Cao: "The realm is on the brink of chaos. Without a man of age-saving talent, it cannot be saved. He who can settle it—is it not you?" He Yong of Nanyang, having seen Cao, said: "The House of Han is doomed to fall; he who shall settle the realm must surely be this man." Xu Shao of Runan had a name for the discerning of men. Cao went to see him and asked: "What manner of man am I?" Shao gave no answer. He asked again, and Shao said: "You are an able minister in an age of order, and a treacherous hero in an age of chaos." Cao heard this with great delight. At twenty, raised by filial fame, he was made a Gentleman of the Palace, and appointed Northern Commandant of Luoyang. On first taking office, he set up more than ten cudgels of five colors at the four gates of the district. Whoever offended against the prohibitions, no matter how powerful or noble, was punished without exception. The uncle of the Permanent Attendant Jian Shuo, walking at night with a sword, was seized by Cao on patrol and chastised with the cudgel. From that time, no one within or without durst offend, and his fame and authority shook the country greatly. Later he became Magistrate of Dunqiu. When the Yellow Turbans rose, he was appointed Cavalry Commandant, and led five thousand horse and foot to come to Yingchuan to aid in the fight. It happened just as Zhang Liang and Zhang Bao were fleeing in defeat: Cao Cao intercepted them, made a great slaughter, beheading more than ten thousand, and capturing banners, gold drums, and horses in great abundance. Zhang Liang and Zhang Bao broke clear by desperate combat. Cao met Huangfu Song and Zhu Jun, and at once led his troops in pursuit of Zhang Liang and Zhang Bao.
paragraphs.rhyme:
In [Cao](char-cao-cao)'s own day, Qiao Xuan, of seer's renown,
Thus spoke to [Cao](char-cao-cao): "The realm shall soon be down.
None save a man of age-redeeming might
Can pacify — that man art thou aright."
He Yong of Nanyang, on the youth he gazed,
Pronounced: "The Han is fall'n: her glory razed.
He who shall give the troubled realm its rest
Is this same man — in him our hopes invest."
Of Runan came Xu Shao, of fame profound
For reading men — [Cao](char-cao-cao) sought his judgment sound.
[Cao](char-cao-cao) asked: "What sort of man am I, I pray?"
Shao spoke not, mute he stood, made no display.
He asked again; whereon Shao made reply:
"In peace, a minister of merit high;
In chaos, crafty hero, full of guile."
[Cao](char-cao-cao) heard the words, and broke into a smile.
At twenty, by his filial fame he came
A Gentleman, and earned the courtly name.
Then Northern Commandant of [Luoyang](loc-luoyang)'s town,
He held the seat that court had handed down.
On taking office, more than ten he made:
Five-colored cudgels at the four gates laid.
Whoever broke the law, of high or low,
Was struck with rod, and felt the heavy blow.
[Jian Shuo](char-jian-shuo)'s own uncle, sword at night, was found
By [Cao](char-cao-cao) on patrol, who held law's strict ground:
The cudgel's stroke he took — high though his stand;
No rank could buy escape from law's stern hand.
From thence none durst, within the walls or out,
Transgress; [Cao](char-cao-cao)'s name shook all the realm about.
[Cao](char-cao-cao) thence to Dunqiu's office took his stand,
A Magistrate, by edict of the land.
When Yellow Turbans rose, the court him call'd,
And as Commandant of the Horse install'd.
With horse and foot, five thousand strong he led,
And on toward Yingchuan he swiftly sped.
There, just as [Liang](char-zhang-liang) and [Bao](char-zhang-bao) in flight fell back,
[Cao Cao](char-cao-cao) met them, and stopped their breaking track,
And made a slaughter great — ten thousand fell;
And captured banners, drums, and steeds as well.
Yet [Liang](char-zhang-liang) and [Bao](char-zhang-bao), by deeds of desp'rate fight,
Broke through [Cao](char-cao-cao)'s ranks, and saved themselves in flight.
With [Song](char-huangfu-song) and [Zhu Jun](char-zhu-jun) met, [Cao](char-cao-cao) made no stay,
But led his troops to chase the brothers' way.

paragraphs.original: 卻說玄德引關、張來潁川，聽得喊殺之聲，又望見火光燭天，急引兵來時，賊已敗散。玄德見皇甫嵩，朱雋，其道盧植之意。嵩曰：「張梁、張寶勢窮力乏，必投廣宗去依張角。玄德可即星夜往助。」
paragraphs.prose: Now Xuande, leading Guan and Zhang, came on toward Yingchuan, where they heard the cries of slaughter and saw the firelight that lit the heavens. They hurried their troops forward, but by the time they arrived, the rebels had already been broken and scattered. Xuande met Huangfu Song and Zhu Jun, and laid before them Lu Zhi's intent. Song said: "Zhang Liang and Zhang Bao, with their force exhausted and their strength spent, will surely make for Guangzong to take refuge with Zhang Jiao. Xuande, you may go at once by night to aid him."
paragraphs.rhyme:
Meanwhile [Liu Bei](char-liu-bei), with [Guan](char-guan-yu) and [Zhang](char-zhang-fei), drew nigh
To Yingchuan's plain, to where the smoke rose high.
They heard the cries of slaughter from afar,
And saw the firelight reach the highest star.
They urged their troops in haste, and onward sped;
But when they came, the rebels all had fled.
[Liu Bei](char-liu-bei) met [Song](char-huangfu-song) and [Zhu Jun](char-zhu-jun), and made known
The plan and purpose that his chief had shown.
Said [Song](char-huangfu-song): "The brothers, of their force bereft,
To Guangzong fly, where [Zhang Jiao](char-zhang-jiao) yet is left.
Go thou at once, by starlight march away,
To aid [Lu Zhi](char-lu-zhi), ere comes another day."

paragraphs.original: 玄德領命，遂引兵復回。到得半路，只見一簇軍馬，護送一輛檻車，車中之囚，乃盧植也。玄德大驚，滾鞍下馬，問其緣故。植曰：「我圍張角，將次可破；因角用妖術，未能即勝。朝廷差黃門左豐前來體探，問我索取賄賂。我答曰：『軍糧尚缺，安有餘錢奉承天使？』左豐挾恨，回奏朝廷，說我高壘不戰，惰慢軍心；因此朝廷震怒，遣中郎將董卓來代將我兵，取我回京問罪。」
paragraphs.prose: Xuande received the order, and forthwith led his troops back. Halfway along the road, they came upon a band of soldiers escorting a prison-cart; the prisoner within was Lu Zhi himself. Xuande was thunderstruck, and rolling from his saddle, asked the reason. Lu Zhi said: "I had Zhang Jiao all but surrounded, and his fall was at hand; but because Jiao practiced sorcery, I could not at once gain the victory. The court sent the Yellow Gate eunuch Zuo Feng to inspect, and he demanded a bribe of me. I answered: 'Our army's grain is yet short—how should I have surplus money to flatter the imperial envoy?' Zuo Feng held a grudge, and returning, reported to the court that I sat behind high walls and would not fight, slackening the spirit of my men. Whereon the court was wroth, and sent General of the Household Dong Zhuo to take over my troops in my place, and to bring me back to the capital to be charged."
paragraphs.rhyme:
[Liu Bei](char-liu-bei) obeyed the charge, and turned his train,
Marched back to Guangzong's road in haste again.
Half on the way, an escort-train they met,
And [Lu Zhi](char-lu-zhi), shackled, in the cart was set.
[Liu Bei](char-liu-bei), struck through with shock, came down with speed,
And asked [Lu Zhi](char-lu-zhi) the cause of this dread deed.
Said [Lu Zhi](char-lu-zhi): "I had pressed [Zhang Jiao](char-zhang-jiao) so close
That naught remained but breaking him with blows;
But by his sorcery he held the field,
And I could not at once compel to yield.
From court Zuo Feng was sent, of [Yellow Gate](misc-yellow-gate),
To view our camp, and bribe demanded straight.
I answered: 'Grain itself is yet to find;
What spare have I to feed the envoy's mind?'
Zuo Feng with malice to the court appeal'd,
And falsely charged that I had spurn'd the field:
Behind tall walls, said he, I idle lay,
And slacken'd all my soldiers day by day.
The court in wrath then sent [Dong Zhuo](char-dong-zhuo) to take
My troops, and fetch me back for trial's sake."

paragraphs.original: 張飛聽罷，大怒，要斬護送軍人，以救盧植。玄德急止之曰：「朝廷自有公論，汝豈可造次？」軍士簇擁盧植去了。關公曰：「盧中郎已被逮，別人領兵，我等去無所依，不如且回涿郡。」玄德從其言，遂引軍北行。
paragraphs.prose: Zhang Fei, having heard, was greatly enraged, and would have beheaded the escort to deliver Lu Zhi. Xuande hastily checked him: "The court has its own public judgment—how can you act so rashly?" The soldiers crowded Lu Zhi away. Lord Guan said: "General Lu has already been seized; another now leads the troops; if we go on, we shall have none on whom to lean. Better, for the moment, to return to Zhuo Commandery." Xuande followed his counsel, and led his troops northward.
paragraphs.rhyme:
[Zhang Fei](char-zhang-fei), on hearing, fired with rage, drew steel,
To slay the guards, and [Lu Zhi](char-lu-zhi)'s bonds unseal.
[Liu Bei](char-liu-bei) in haste held off: "The court will scan
With public eye — rash deed becomes no man."
The guards in throng escorted [Lu Zhi](char-lu-zhi) past,
And bore him onward to his prison fast.
Then [Guan Yu](char-guan-yu) said: "[Lu Zhi](char-lu-zhi) is captive ta'en;
Another leads — to march were march in vain.
Far better turn us back to [Zhuo](loc-zhuo) with speed,
Than wander on with none our cause to lead."
[Liu Bei](char-liu-bei) agreed, and turning to the north,
Led his small host, and back to [Zhuo](loc-zhuo) set forth.

paragraphs.original: 行無二日，忽聞山後喊聲大震。玄德引關、張縱馬上高岡望之，見漢軍大敗，後面漫山塞野，黃巾蓋地而來，旗上大書「天公將軍」。玄德曰：「此張角也！可速戰！」
paragraphs.prose: They had marched scarcely two days when from behind a mountain there suddenly arose a great clamor of cries. Xuande, leading Guan and Zhang, urged his horse up a high mound and looked. He saw the Han army utterly defeated, and behind them, swarming over hill and field, came a host of Yellow Turbans, with banners on which was writ in large characters: "General of the Lord of Heaven." Xuande said: "This is Zhang Jiao! We must fight at once!"
paragraphs.rhyme:
Ere two days passed, behind a hill they heard
A sudden clamor's outcry, fierce and stirred.
[Liu Bei](char-liu-bei) led [Guan](char-guan-yu) and [Zhang](char-zhang-fei) up to a height,
And there beheld the Han host put to flight.
Behind, the Yellow Turbans, like a tide,
Pour'd over hill and field, with banners wide.
And on the flags one mighty name was traced:
'The General of Heaven,' boldly placed.
Said [Liu Bei](char-liu-bei): "'Tis [Zhang Jiao](char-zhang-jiao)! Strike him in haste!"

paragraphs.original: 三人飛馬引軍而出。張角正殺敗董卓，乘勢趕來，忽遇三人衝殺，角軍大亂，敗走五十餘里。三人救了董卓回寨。卓問三人現居何職。玄德曰：「白身。」卓甚輕之，不為禮。玄德出，張飛大怒曰：「我等親赴血戰，救了這廝，他卻如此無禮﹔若不殺之，難消我氣！」便要提刀入帳來殺董卓。正是：人情勢利古猶今，誰識英雄是白身？安得快人如翼德，盡誅世上負心人！畢竟董卓性命如何，且看下文分解。
paragraphs.prose: The three rode swift and led their men forth. Zhang Jiao at that moment had just routed Dong Zhuo and was pressing the pursuit, when suddenly he met the charge of the three. His army fell into wild disorder, and fled over fifty li. The three rescued Dong Zhuo and returned with him to camp. Zhuo asked them what offices they presently held. Xuande said: "None—we are commoners." Zhuo treated them with great contempt and showed them no courtesy. When Xuande had gone out, Zhang Fei was filled with wrath: "We have ourselves gone into bloody battle and rescued this wretch, yet he uses us thus discourteously! If I do not kill him, my anger will not be appeased!" And he took up his sword and would enter the tent to slay Dong Zhuo. Truly: "The ways of men, swayed by power and profit, were the same in olden days as now; / who can know a hero clothed as a commoner? / Where shall one find a quick-tempered man like Yide, / to slay all the world's ingrates?" As to what should become of Dong Zhuo's life, see the next chapter for the resolution.
paragraphs.rhyme:
Forth flew the three, with troops behind them led;
[Zhang Jiao](char-zhang-jiao), with [Dong Zhuo](char-dong-zhuo) routed, onward sped.
He met the three, who, sudden, charged amain;
His army, broken, scatter'd o'er the plain.
Full fifty li and more they fled in pain.
They sav'd [Dong Zhuo](char-dong-zhuo), and back to camp they went,
And brought him safely to his command-tent.
[Zhuo](char-dong-zhuo) asked their rank. [Liu Bei](char-liu-bei) replied with grace:
"Mere commoners we are — no rank, no place."
[Zhuo](char-dong-zhuo), hearing this, in scorn forbore his praise,
And show'd no courtesy, but turn'd his gaze.
[Liu Bei](char-liu-bei) withdrew; whereon [Zhang Fei](char-zhang-fei) broke out
In passion's fire, and rais'd a mighty shout:
"We risked our lives in bloody fray to save
This wretch, who treats us thus, ungrateful knave!
Unless I slay him, ne'er my rage shall stay."
He grasp'd his blade — to the chief's tent his way.
The ways of men, by gain and power led,
Forget the hero in a common stead.
How shall we find a [Zhang Fei](char-zhang-fei), fierce to slay
All ingrate hearts upon the earth today?
And what of [Dong Zhuo](char-dong-zhuo)'s life shall now befall?
The next account shall make it plain to all.
